paras: Today we read a wise tale about a farmer who grew fruits. We will also test which fruits float or sink, learn opposite words, practise using 'is' and 'are', and do some maths with fruits.

Once upon a time, there was a farmer who liked fruits. So, he decided to grow fruits on his land. He worked hard to grow a variety of fruits. With hard work and care, the trees grew well. He took special care to grow grapes and watermelons in a small corner of his farm.

When the fruits were all ripe and ready to be eaten, the farmer decided to gift the best fruit to the king. Then his wife said, “This year, the best fruits on our farm are the watermelons and the grapes.” The farmer thought about it and said, “Since it is a long journey to the palace, I shall take the grapes as watermelons are too heavy.” So, he put bunches of grapes in a basket and walked to the king’s palace.

sections.heading: A. What do you think will happen next?

items.q: The farmer is carrying a basket of grapes to the palace. What do you think will happen next? Say it aloud.
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended prediction. Accept any sensible answer, for example, 'The King will like the grapes' or 'The King will give him a reward'. Let children check their guess after reading the story.

paras: The farmer reached the palace. He told the palace guard that he had brought a gift for the King. The palace guard then took him to the royal garden. The farmer saw the King playing with the princess. So, he quietly kept the basket full of grapes in front of him and sat down.

When the King sat down to rest, the guard brought the basket of grapes to the King. The guard pointed to the farmer and told the King that the grapes were a gift from the farmer. The King saw the farmer. The King was still in a playful mood. He took a bunch of grapes from the basket. He plucked out one grape and popped it into his mouth. Then he plucked another grape and threw it playfully at the farmer.
When the grape hit the farmer’s forehead, he said, “Thank God!”
The King was surprised! He threw a grape again.
The farmer again said, “Thank God! I am blessed!”
The King asked the farmer, “Why are you thanking God when I am throwing grapes at you?”

The wise farmer replied with a smile, “O mighty King! I had grown the best grapes and watermelons on my farm. I chose the grapes to gift to you. Imagine if I had brought watermelons! Indeed, God is great!”
— A Jataka tale
New words: journey, guard, royal, popped, wise
Sight words: grow, kept, front, again

sections.heading: B. Answer the following.

items.q: 1. What did the farmer grow on his farm?
items.a: He grew a variety of fruits. He took special care to grow grapes and watermelons.

items.q: 2. What did his wife say?
items.a: She said that the best fruits on their farm that year were the watermelons and the grapes.

items.q: 3. Why did the farmer decide to take the grapes?
items.a: The journey to the palace was long, and watermelons were too heavy to carry.

items.q: 4. What did the King do playfully?
items.a: He plucked a grape and threw it at the farmer. (He also popped one grape into his mouth.)

items.q: 5. Why did the farmer say, ‘Thank God’?
items.a: He was thankful that he had brought grapes and not watermelons. A watermelon thrown at him would have hurt very much.

sections.heading: C. Think and say.

items.q: 1. The farmer in the story grew fruits. What else can a farmer grow?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, wheat, rice, vegetables, cotton, sugarcane, flowers).

items.q: 2. Are there women farmers? Do you know any?
items.a: Teacher note: Yes, many women work as farmers. Let children share examples from their family or village.

items.q: 3. If you meet a farmer, what would you say to them?
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended. Encourage polite sentences, for example, 'Thank you for growing our food.'

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Counting the grapes

items.q: A bunch has 12 grapes. The King popped 1 grape into his mouth and threw 2 grapes at the farmer. How many grapes were left in the bunch?
items.a: 1 + 2 = 3 grapes were used. 12 - 3 = 9 grapes were left.

items.q: The 9 grapes that are left are shared equally among the King, the princess and the guard. How many grapes does each get?
items.a: 9 divided by 3 = 3 grapes each.

paras: The farmer knew that watermelons are heavy and grapes are light. Let us become young scientists and find out how fruits behave when we put them in water and when we weigh them. Use a tub of water, a watermelon, a few grapes and a simple balance (or a weighing scale).

sections.heading: D. Float or Sink? Predict first, then try the experiment with your teacher.
sections.note: Teacher note: Ask children to write their prediction first and then record what they actually observe. A whole watermelon usually floats, and a grape usually sinks. Results can vary with the size and ripeness of the fruit. Remember that in Lesson 10 we learnt that a heavy object does not always sink.

items.q: Will a grape float or sink?
items.a: A grape usually sinks.

items.q: Will a whole watermelon float or sink?
items.a: A whole watermelon usually floats, even though it is much heavier than a grape.

items.q: Is a heavy object always going to sink? Why was your prediction right or wrong?
items.a: Teacher note: No. Heavy objects can float, as a big ship does. Children should explain in simple words based on what they saw.

sections.heading: E. Heavy and Light. Use the balance.
sections.note: Teacher note: Place a watermelon on one side of the balance and a few grapes on the other side. The heavier side goes down. Do not throw fruits at anyone. Only discuss the next question.

items.q: Which side of the balance went down, the watermelon side or the grape side?
items.a: The watermelon side, because it is heavier.

items.q: Which fruit is lighter: a grape or a watermelon?
items.a: A grape.

items.q: Think about the story. Which would hurt more if it were thrown at you, a grape or a watermelon? Why?
items.a: A watermelon would hurt more because it is much heavier. Heavy things hit harder.

paras: The farmer knew that the watermelon was heavy and the grapes were light. The words heavy and light are opposite in meaning.
Look at the pictures: a thick book and a thin book, a long journey and a short walk, soft cotton and a hard rock, a slow tortoise and a fast rabbit.
The ball is round.
The tables are brown.

Look at the pictures and fill in the blanks with ‘is’ or ‘are’. Pictures: giraffes and a rabbit in a jungle, a wooden table, three yellow mangoes, a tall boy looking at a flower, a teddy bear and a ball on a shelf, a red book on a table, two girls at a shop, a blue car on a road.

sections.heading: F. Write the opposite of the word in brackets.

items.q: thick book - ______ book (thick)
items.a: thin

items.q: long journey - ______ journey (long)
items.a: short

items.q: soft cotton - ______ rock (soft)
items.a: hard

items.q: slow tortoise - ______ rabbit (slow)
items.a: fast

items.q: Write the opposite of the word ‘heavy’.
items.a: light

sections.heading: G. Read the sentences.
sections.note: The ball is round. The tables are brown.

items.q: In ‘The ball is round’, how many balls are there? Which word do we use: is or are?
items.a: One ball. We use ‘is’.

items.q: In ‘The tables are brown’, how many tables are there? Which word do we use: is or are?
items.a: More than one table. We use ‘are’.

sections.heading: H. Fill in the blanks with ‘is’ or ‘are’.

items.q: 1. There ________ animals in the jungle.
items.a: are

items.q: 2. The table ________ made of wood.
items.a: is

items.q: 3. These mangoes ________ sweet.
items.a: are

items.q: 4. Raghuram ________ a tall boy.
items.a: is

items.q: 5. The toys ________ on the shelf.
items.a: are

items.q: 6. The book ________ on the table.
items.a: is

items.q: 7. The girls ________ at the shop.
items.a: are

items.q: 8. The car ________ on the road.
items.a: is

sections.heading: Science Corner: Hard or soft?
sections.note: Teacher note: Let children touch real objects in the classroom and decide.

items.q: Write hard or soft: a pillow, a brick, cotton, a stone.
items.a: Pillow - soft; brick - hard; cotton - soft; stone - hard.

items.q: Is a watermelon hard or soft on the outside? And a grape?
items.a: Teacher note: A watermelon is hard on the outside, and a grape is soft. Children should say what they feel.

paras: Aachoo!

Once a mighty elephant,
Got a mighty cold.
It went to buy a handkerchief,
Where handkerchiefs were sold.

“A hanky for an elephant?”
The sales girl was surprised,
“Sorry sir but we don’t have
A handkerchief that size.”

“AACHOO!” said the elephant.
And shook its mighty head,
“Forget about the handkerchief
Give me a sheet instead.”
Imagine you are visiting the Big Elephant. You know that the elephant has a cold. What food items will you take with you? Say them aloud.

sections.heading: I. Answer the following about the poem.

items.q: 1. Why did the elephant go to the shop?
items.a: It had a cold and wanted to buy a handkerchief.

items.q: 2. Why was the sales girl surprised?
items.a: She had never been asked for a handkerchief for an elephant.

items.q: 3. What did the elephant ask for instead of a handkerchief?
items.a: A sheet.

items.q: 4. Find the words in the poem that rhyme with ‘cold’, ‘surprised’ and ‘head’.
items.a: cold - sold; surprised - size; head - instead.

sections.heading: J. Imagine and say.

items.q: What food items will you take with you to the elephant who has a cold?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Sample: oranges, lemons, apples, warm soup, warm water. Talk about which foods are healthy.

items.q: Sort the items from the picture: grapes, pumpkin, corn, lemons, watermelon, apples. Which are fruits and which are vegetables?
items.a: Fruits: grapes, lemons, watermelon, apples. Vegetables: pumpkin, corn. (Teacher note: Accept corn as a vegetable or a grain.)

sections.heading: Science Corner: Air and sound
sections.note: Teacher note: Give each child a small strip of paper or a feather. Ask them to blow gently and then blow hard on it.

items.q: What happens to the paper strip when you blow gently? And when you blow hard?
items.a: It moves a little when we blow gently and a lot when we blow hard. Moving air can push things.

items.q: A sneeze like ‘Aachoo!’ pushes out a lot of air very fast. Why should we cover our mouth and nose when we sneeze?
items.a: So that germs do not spread to other people. Use a handkerchief or the elbow.

items.q: Say ‘Aachoo!’ in a loud voice and then in a soft voice. Which sound can people far away hear?
items.a: The loud sound.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: A sheet for the elephant
sections.note: Teacher note: Give each child a handkerchief or a piece of cloth and a ruler.

items.q: Measure your handkerchief in hand-spans and then in centimetres. How long is it?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. A typical handkerchief is about 30 cm to 40 cm long. Let children compare their hand-span measures.

items.q: A handkerchief is 30 cm long. The elephant’s sheet is 5 times as long. How long is the sheet?
items.a: 30 x 5 = 150 cm (1 metre and 50 centimetres).

paras: Chandu’s Fruit Salad
Chandu has written the steps for preparing a salad on a few slips of paper. He mixed them up. Think of the proper order and write down in the space given below.

sections.heading: K. Put the steps in the right order. Write 1 to 7 in the brackets.

items.q: ( ) Next, I put in papaya cubes.
( ) Mother cuts some fruits for me.
( ) First I take some banana slices.
( ) Finally, I squeeze a lemon on it, adding a pinch of salt.
( ) Then I add the apple slices.
( ) Then I mix them all.
( ) After that I add some grapes from a bunch.

sections.heading: L. Write the steps of your favourite fruit salad or juice in 3 to 5 sentences.

items.q: Use the words first, next, then and finally.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept any correct sequence of steps. Sample: First, I wash the fruits. Next, I cut them. Then I put them in a bowl. Finally, I eat the salad.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: First, second, third

items.q: Chandu adds banana, papaya, apple and grapes in that order. Which fruit is added 3rd?
items.a: Apple.

items.q: Which fruit is added 4th?
items.a: Grapes.

items.q: An apple is cut into 4 equal parts. What do we call each part?
items.a: A quarter.

items.q: Chandu uses 2 of the 4 equal parts of the apple. What fraction of the apple is that?
items.a: Half (2 out of 4 parts, or two quarters).

paras: Now let us find fruits hidden in a grid of letters. Words can go across or down.

sections.heading: M. Find fruits in the grid given below.
sections.note: Teacher note: Add the grid as a picture, or write it on the board. Grid rows: S M F X C U D M / P A P A Y A H G / E N G K S B T U / A G R A P E S A / R O Z D H Y L V / A X B A N A N A / Z P E A C H O G / P L U M H Q P W. Words to find: MANGO, PAPAYA, GRAPES, BANANA, GUAVA, PLUM, PEACH, PEAR.

items.q: MANGO
items.a: Down, starting at M in the top row (2nd letter).

items.q: PAPAYA
items.a: Across, row 2, starting from the left.

items.q: GRAPES
items.a: Across, row 4, starting at the 2nd letter.

items.q: BANANA
items.a: Across, row 6, starting at the 3rd letter.

items.q: GUAVA
items.a: Down, in the last column, starting in row 2.

items.q: PLUM
items.a: Across, the bottom row, starting from the left.

items.q: PEACH
items.a: Across, row 7, starting at the 2nd letter.

items.q: PEAR
items.a: Down, in the first column, starting in row 2.

sections.heading: N. Write the 8 fruit names in alphabetical order (A to Z).

items.a: BANANA, GRAPES, GUAVA, MANGO, PAPAYA, PEACH, PEAR, PLUM.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Count and chart

items.q: How many fruit names have 5 letters? Name them.
items.a: 3 names: MANGO, GUAVA, PEACH.

items.q: How many fruit names have 6 letters? Name them.
items.a: 3 names: PAPAYA, GRAPES, BANANA.

items.q: Class survey: Ask each child to name their favourite fruit. Make tally marks on the board. Which fruit got the most votes?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary with the class. Help children count the tally marks and, if time permits, draw a simple bar chart.
